channel.title: Personal News Feed — News & World Affairs
channel.description: Personally scored news, world affairs, opinion/analysis & foreign affairs, business & finance, and San Diego/local articles curated by news-filter

item.title: Air Pollution May Alter Brain Structure and Increase Dementia Risk
item.description:
Source: Washington Post Original headline: A remarkable new picture is emerging of how the air around us could alter the brain
Air pollution may alter brain structure and increase dementia risk. Researchers found microplastics, silica, metals, and soot in brain tissue from deceased individuals, with some particles reaching the amygdala. Studies link PM2.5 exposure to higher dementia risk, with one UK Biobank study showing a 14% increased risk for those with highest exposure. Brain scans revealed reduced brain volumes in polluted areas. Another study found PM2.5 exposure correlated with hippocampal changes, involving inflammation and fat metabolism. A 2025 Science study linked pollution to Lewy body dementia via alpha-synuclein buildup in mice. Metals in diesel exhaust and World Trade Center dust triggered similar genetic changes, suggesting their role in brain damage. Caleb Finch noted pollution’s cumulative effect over a lifetime. Xiaobo Mao highlighted metals’ potential harm and emphasized controlling exposure through HVAC filters, diet, and avoiding high-traffic areas. The findings underscore the need to understand pollution’s direct impact on the brain.

item.title: Wait: Your autonomous Tesla won't drive everywhere just yet
item.description:
Source: Business Insider
Tesla's Full Self-Driving software will offer unsupervised autonomy in early 2025 with FSD V15, but only in areas where its Robotaxi service operates. VP of AI Ashok Elluswamy said the feature will be available in parts of seven U.S. cities: Austin, Dallas, Houston, Miami, Orlando, Tampa, and the San Francisco Bay Area. The Robotaxi platform, which includes supervised operations in the Bay Area, defines the geofenced zones where Tesla claims the technology is safe. Customers must have vehicles within these zones to use the feature. Elluswamy emphasized that autonomy remains a complex challenge, dismissing competitors' ability to catch up. Other companies like Tensor also plan geofenced self-driving features. Tesla did not explain why geofencing is required, though liability concerns may play a role. The rollout marks a step toward broader autonomy but with significant geographic limitations.

item.title: Sundar Pichai explains how a team of AI agents helps him run the company
item.description:
Source: Business Insider
Google CEO Sundar Pichai uses AI agents to manage information-gathering tasks. During a podcast interview, Pichai explained that agents summarize daily updates, track computing resource usage, and monitor internal communications, reducing his need to manually review data. He emphasized that while agents provide insights, humans retain control over critical decisions. Managing these agents has become a new responsibility, causing increased task-switching and workload for some employees. A Cisco engineer noted overseeing multiple agents intensifies work without reducing hours. Pichai highlighted the advantage of continuous 24/7 operation, allowing agents to handle tasks between human shifts. He described the process as a 'continuum' where agents pick up where users left off, enabling focused problem-solving. Despite benefits, challenges include preventing duplication and ensuring agents stay within their assigned roles.

item.title: High health costs strain workers despite employer-provided insurance
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: News Original headline: High health costs squeeze workers, even if you have good insurance through a job
Joseph Babbitt, a 60-year-old worker with employer-provided health insurance, says high deductibles — now averaging $5,000 annually — make care unaffordable despite free premiums. A KFF report shows family health insurance premiums rose 5% in 2026, with workers paying $7,000 annually on average. Matthew Rae of KFF notes that 9% growth in worker-paid premiums could shift costs to employees. A Commonwealth Fund survey found 43% of insured workers skipped care due to cost, and 31% had medical debt. Uninsured rates rose as federal subsidies for ACA plans expired and Medicaid coverage ended post-pandemic. Sara Collins of the Commonwealth Fund highlights growing coverage losses, with millions projected to lose Medicaid next year. Public support for federal action on affordability and coverage remains strong, with 76% of independents and 45% of Republicans agreeing the government should ensure coverage for all Americans.

item.title: Gen Z Less Likely to Have Kids Than Older Generations at 26
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: One chart shows how Gen Zers are way less likely to have kids than older generations at their age
Birth rates in the US have declined, with Gen Zers in their 20s significantly less likely to have children than older generations at the same age. A Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta analysis shows 26% of Gen Zers plan to have at least one child, compared to 47% of millennials, 50% of Gen X, and 46% of boomers. Researchers controlled for education, partnership status, and health conditions using National Survey of Family Growth data up to 2023. Medical challenges like impaired fecundity also contribute, with 18% of Gen Zers at 26 facing fertility issues versus 10% of boomers. Financial costs, including $303,418 in child-rearing expenses over 18 years, are another barrier. Gen Zer Brooklen Farley cited economic and climate concerns, while millennial Lizzie Lawson noted rising costs and reduced family support. Michael Konczal noted declining large families across income levels. The US fertility rate is 1.6 births per woman, below the replacement rate of 2.1. The Congressional Budget Office projects US births could fall below deaths by the early 2030s, leading to population decline by 2056.

item.title: Africa CDC Convenes Crisis Meeting Amid Ebola Spread
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Original headline: Africa CDC calls crisis meeting as Ebola spreads
Africa's Center for Disease Control (CDC) announced an extraordinary virtual meeting of national health officials as the Ebola outbreak spreads across the continent. Over 9,500 infections and nearly half fatalities have been reported since the virus was detected in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) in May. Nigeria confirmed a case linked to a woman returning from Uganda, prompting contact tracing of 44 individuals. Uganda, which declared itself Ebola-free in July, rejected Nigeria's claims, while the World Health Organization (WHO) declared its outbreak over on August 27. The current outbreak involves the rare Bundibugyo virus, with no approved vaccines or treatments, confirmed in both Nigeria and Uganda. Africa CDC Director Dr. Jean Kaseya emphasized the need for urgent action, noting the outbreak now affects three African regions. The WHO urged regional countries to maintain high readiness as the DRC outbreak evolves. A French doctor infected in Congo recovered after treatment in France. The crisis meeting aims to strengthen collective response and mobilize African resources to combat the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record.

item.title: Psychedelics Show Inflammation Reduction in Parkinson's Patients
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: Science Original headline: New human data hints at psychedelics' potential to combat inflammation
New research suggests psychedelics like psilocybin may reduce inflammation in Parkinson's patients. A study published in JAMA Psychiatry measured inflammation markers in 12 participants before and after psilocybin sessions. Participants showed significantly lower inflammation levels post-treatment, with some improvements persisting a month later. Blood tests also indicated reduced mitochondrial stress. Dr. Ellen Bradley noted the findings provide an initial biological signal for further investigation. Researchers caution the study lacks a control group and participants knew they received the drug, emphasizing the need for follow-up studies. Aoife O'Donovan called the results 'objective markers' supporting continued research. Parkinson's involves inflammation and mitochondrial dysfunction, which may explain the observed benefits. The study could inform treatments for other inflammatory diseases. Previous animal studies showed psychedelics' anti-inflammatory effects, but human validation is needed. Charles Nichols, whose lab discovered psychedelics' anti-inflammatory properties years ago, called the study a 'proof of principle' for future research.

item.title: Dream incubation offers problem-solving insights through targeted dreaming
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: News Original headline: Can a dream help you solve a problem? Here's how to try tonight
Dream incubation, an ancient practice of planting questions before sleep to gain insights, is gaining renewed scientific interest. Researchers note that while early psychiatrists dismissed dreams as random, psychologist Rosalind Cartwright argued for their therapeutic potential. Modern studies, including a 1990s Harvard experiment, suggest focused dreaming may offer solutions. Jungian analyst Lisa Marchiano advises asking open-ended questions, like 'What would it look like if I took this job?' and preparing mentally before sleep. She recommends writing down known information to invite unconscious insights. Dr. Harrison Shong-Wen Chow highlights the importance of dream recall, noting people often forget within minutes. His research explores how dreams under anesthesia might process trauma. Practical steps include setting intentions, using rituals like writing questions on paper, and keeping a notebook. While results vary, the practice may foster new perspectives over time.

item.title: AI Agents as Sellable Business Services for Entrepreneurs and Agencies
item.description:
Source: San Diego Reader stories Original headline: AI Acquisition turns AI agents into sellable business services for entrepreneurs and agencies
AI Acquisition, a Dubai-based company, offers an AI business operating system that packages specialized agents into sellable services for entrepreneurs and agencies. Founded by Jordan Lee, the platform streamlines business functions like outreach, sales, client communication, and growth planning without requiring large teams. Agents handle tasks such as lead generation, cold email campaigns, website creation, and account management, enabling operators to deliver structured workflows as services. Lee argues that AI’s true value lies in integrating with existing business processes rather than standalone tools. He emphasizes that agents should act as dedicated roles, not just gadgets, with clear responsibilities and measurable outcomes. The platform includes tools like AI Niche Researcher, AI Growth Consultant, and AI Account Manager, structured to guide businesses from market analysis to customer retention. Lee stresses that while AI can automate repetitive tasks, human oversight remains critical for trust-building and strategic decisions. AI Acquisition positions itself as a shift toward practical, accessible AI services, allowing non-technical entrepreneurs to leverage AI for scalable business growth.

item.title: U.S. Secretary Rubio Focuses on Business in India Trip
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Original headline: In India, Rubio Is All Business
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio embarked on a three-day trip to India, skipping New Delhi to focus on commercial interests. His itinerary included Mumbai and Jamnagar, where he met with Indian officials and business leaders, including Reliance Industries’ Mukesh Ambani. Rubio emphasized energy cooperation, noting India’s diversified oil imports and the Trump administration’s pause on sanctions against countries purchasing Russian oil. He also laid a wreath in honor of the 2008 Mumbai terrorist attack victims, highlighting past U.S.-India counterterrorism collaboration. Indian External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar met Rubio in Mumbai, signaling New Delhi’s prioritization of U.S. ties despite trust gaps. Meanwhile, the full text of the Mecca pact between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey was revealed, containing NATO-like mutual defense language. In Saudi Arabia, two Bangladeshis were executed for offenses in a Mecca mosque, prompting concerns over diplomatic relations. A Reuters investigation highlighted Bangladesh’s measles crisis, with over 202,000 suspected cases and 1,147 deaths, attributed to political instability and inadequate vaccination efforts.

item.title: Pope Leo XIV Resumes Public Duties After Lung Cancer Surgery
item.description:
Source: BBC News, Deutsche Welle Original headline: Pope Leo XIV to Resume Public Duties After Lung Cancer Surgery
Pope Leo XIV will not require further cancer treatment after successful surgery to remove a lung tumor. Doctors confirmed the 71-year-old pontiff was discharged from Rome's Gemelli Hospital on October 17 following a procedure on October 13 to excise the lower lobe of his right lung. Test results showed the growth was a localized lung adenocarcinoma, with no need for additional therapy. Doctors Dr. Luigi Carbone and Professor Stefano Margaritora stated there is 'no clinical reason to cancel' his planned South America trip. The pope first disclosed his condition during a Sunday blessing on October 11, revealing a lung nodule. During his hospital stay, he celebrated Mass from Gemelli Hospital, wore green vestments, and engaged in diplomatic calls with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. The Vatican emphasized his recovery allows him to proceed with a November Latin America visit to Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru, involving multiple flights and high-altitude locations. His discharge coincided with his first weekly general audience since the surgery at St. Peter's Square.

item.title: Storm brings rain and surf warnings to Southern California
item.description:
Source: LA Times Original headline: New storm moves into Southern California: What to expect
A new storm is moving into Southern California Wednesday, bringing moderate rain from late morning to Thursday afternoon. The National Weather Service forecasts a 30% to 40% chance of thunderstorms, with widespread minor flooding and debris flow risks in Los Angeles and Ventura counties. The Santa Monica Mountains face the highest flood risk. Rain chances vary by location: Irvine and Anaheim at 53%, San Clemente 46%, Ontario 44%, and Riverside 40%. Precipitation increases Wednesday evening into Thursday morning, with Anaheim, Irvine, and San Clemente at 95% chance. Surf heights of 3 to 6 feet are expected at L.A. County and Oxnard beaches through Thursday night, with tides up to 6.2 feet. The NWS San Diego office issued a beach hazard warning through 11 p.m., cautioning about rip currents, breaking waves, and dangerous surf. Swimmers are advised to avoid the water to prevent hazardous conditions.

item.title: Nigeria's first Ebola case linked to Uganda holiday
item.description:
Source: BBC News Original headline: Nigeria's first Ebola patient holidayed in Uganda, officials say
Nigeria's first confirmed Ebola case is a 42-year-old woman from Uganda who traveled to Kampala for a holiday. She fell ill three days after returning to Abuja on 3 October, according to Africa CDC head Dr Jean Kaseya. Nigeria's health minister confirmed she spent two and a half weeks in Uganda and made a stop in Ethiopia. She is stable and improving. Authorities have identified 44 contacts and banned 46 people from flights. Surveillance measures include health screenings and tracking at Nigerian airports. Neighboring Cameroon also increased checks. Contacts show no symptoms, and she did not travel beyond Abuja. The Bundibugyo strain, linked to the DRC outbreak, was confirmed. Officials dispute Ugandan claims about her nationality and travel, emphasizing collaboration. Nigeria's health minister expressed confidence in containing the outbreak, citing past success in 2014.

item.title: Meta Ordered to Pay $25 Billion for Privacy Violations in New Mexico
item.description:
Source: BBC News, Deutsche Welle Original headline: Meta Ordered to Pay $25 Billion Over Privacy Violations in New Mexico Case
Meta ordered to pay $25 billion to New Mexico for privacy violations. Judge Francis Mathew ruled the company misled users about data handling from 2010 to 2021. The penalty, the largest ever against Meta, follows prior settlements with California and another state. New Mexico’s case focused on the Cambridge Analytica scandal, where 87 million users’ data was harvested in 2016. A jury found Meta violated consumer laws 43 million times. The judge reduced the proposed $219 billion penalty to $25 billion, citing willful misconduct. Meta’s legal team argued the fine would make operations in New Mexico 'all but impossible' and claimed amounts over $3.45 billion are unconstitutional. New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez called the ruling a 'clear message' that corporations face accountability. The state plans to use funds for education, potentially paying for schools for a century. Prosecutors initially sought $40 billion, while Meta’s lawyers argued for a cap of $3.45 billion. The case highlights ongoing scrutiny of Meta’s data practices and legal pressure on tech companies.

item.title: Two killed in airport attack as Houthi conflict escalates
item.description:
Source: BBC News Original headline: Two killed in attack on airport in eastern Saudi Arabia, authorities say
Two people were killed and eight others injured in an attack at King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, eastern Saudi Arabia, according to the General Authority of Civil Aviation. A Saudi citizen and an Indian resident died, while injured included nationals from Saudi Arabia, India, Yemen, Bangladesh, and Nepal. The attack type remains unspecified, but Yemen's Houthi movement, which has targeted Saudi airports with drones and missiles, is suspected. Earlier Wednesday, debris from an intercepted drone killed two people near Dammam. The Saudi energy ministry reported a drone strike on an Aramco facility in Shaybeh, where a contractor's vehicle was set ablaze. Four additional drones were intercepted later. Houthis claimed attacks on Saudi airports and energy sites as retaliation for air strikes in Yemen. Since October, at least 21 have died in Houthi attacks on Saudi airports, including 13 killed in a missile strike on Riyadh's airport on October 10. The conflict, which began in 2014, has caused over 1,574 deaths and 256,000 displaced people, with fighting continuing in key regions.

item.title: 50 Literary Love Stories Highlighted for Enduring Impact
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic Original headline: 50 Unforgettable Love Stories
A list of 50 literary love stories has been compiled, spanning novels, poetry, plays, and short stories. The selection includes works by authors like Shakespeare, Austen, Brontë, and Sidney, highlighting their enduring impact on literature and language. The list aims to showcase love stories beyond the romance genre, emphasizing their role in shaping cultural and literary traditions. Examples include Sidney’s sonnet sequence about Astrophil and Stella, Shakespeare’s Romeo and Juliet, and Austen’s Persuasion. The compilation reflects a mix of historical and modern works, with some stories featuring dramatic conflicts and emotional depth. The selection process involved scholars, librarians, and authors, focusing on English-language works from the Renaissance onward. Notable entries include epistolary tales, tragic romances, and narratives that explore themes of passion, betrayal, and societal constraints. The list underscores how love stories have influenced idioms, clichés, and literary conventions, remaining relevant across centuries.

item.title: Airbnb bans guests from stripping beds and washing dishes under new rules
item.description:
Source: BBC News Original headline: Airbnb hosts can no longer make guests strip beds and wash dishes under new rules
Airbnb has updated its rules to prevent hosts from asking guests to perform cleaning tasks such as stripping beds or washing dishes. The changes, effective for reservations booked on or after 20 November, limit hosts to seven standard house rules and additional 'reasonable' requests. Airbnb stated guests, who pay a cleaning fee, should not be required to complete tasks typically handled by cleaners. Exceptions include requests related to local water restrictions. Hosts can set rules but cannot impose fines. Violations will be flagged, allowing hosts to appeal. The policy aims to clarify expectations and avoid onerous demands. Critics have long complained about unreasonable tasks, with some hosts facing backlash for strict rules. TikTok videos from hosts Cassie and Jon, showcasing their meticulous inspections, have sparked debate over stringent expectations.

item.title: Neighbor Accused of Feeding Coyote in Toddler Attack Faces Charges
item.description:
Source: LA Times Original headline: Neighbor who allegedly fed a coyote involved in attack on toddler could be charged
A neighbor accused of feeding a coyote involved in a toddler attack faces potential criminal charges. Authorities confirmed the coyote, euthanized in the attack, was responsible for the incident on Glenhurst Avenue. Residents reported the animal as a nuisance since January, with complaints escalating in May and June. Animal control officers visited the neighbor’s home in May but found no evidence of feeding. The case was referred to Los Angeles city attorney’s office after further complaints, though details remain unclear. Officials emphasize that feeding coyotes is illegal and can lead to dangerous behavior, as the animals may lose fear of humans. Experts warn that while coyote attacks on humans are rare—only about 10 nonfatal incidents occur annually in the U.S. and Canada—the risk increases with human interaction. Authorities urge reporting aggressive or fearless coyotes to wildlife officials.

item.title: Two European women freed after over a year in Niger captivity in Libya
item.description:
Source: BBC News Original headline: Two European women held captive for more than a year in Niger freed in Libya
Two women - a Swiss and an Austrian - were freed after more than a year in captivity in Niger and handed over to Libyan authorities in Benghazi. Eva Gretzmacher, 76, and Claudia Abbt, 69, were kidnapped separately in Agadez in January and April 2023. Details about their captors or demands remain undisclosed, though some reports linked the kidnapping to Islamic State militants. Libyan officials stated the women would be transferred to their respective countries after procedures. They thanked Khalifa Haftar and his son Saddam Haftar for their release. Gretzmacher, an aid worker in Niger, and Abbt, a community worker in Agadez, were flown to Vienna for Gretzmacher before continuing to Switzerland. Libya's political division between Haftar's eastern administration and Prime Minister Dbeibah's western government was noted. Analysts cited the return of Tuareg fighters from Gaddafi's forces as a factor in Sahel instability, alongside ongoing jihadist violence in the region. Niger has been under military rule since 2023.

item.title: Starbucks China requires purchases for seating
item.description:
Source: BBC News Original headline: No order, no seat: Starbucks China rolls out new store policy
Starbucks China requires customers to purchase items before sitting in its 8,000 stores starting Thursday. The policy aims to enhance the in-store experience amid competition from local brands like Luckin Coffee. Similar measures have been implemented globally, including restrictions on bulky items in South Korea and a reversal of open-door policies in North America. Chinese social media users largely supported the change, with comments praising reduced seat-hogging and improved seating availability. A previous incident involving chained outdoor seats in Sichuan sparked debate. Starbucks China, now the second-largest market for the company, faces growing competition from Luckin, which overtook Starbucks as China's largest coffee chain in 2023. The company plans to boost staffing and digital systems to manage peak hours. Starbucks sold a 60% stake in its China business to Boyu Capital in a $4bn deal last year.

item.title: 5 Ways to Relieve Desk-Related Aches and Pains
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: News Original headline: 5 simple ways to relieve the aches and pains of sitting at a desk all day
Five methods can alleviate desk-related discomfort. Walking breaks every 30 minutes, as found by Columbia University researchers in 2023, reduce sedentary risks. A 3D T-spine rotation, demonstrated by physical therapist Vinh Pham, relieves back strain by mimicking natural spinal movements. Eye strain from screens can be eased with eye muscle stretches. Changing positions frequently, as advised by biomechanist Katy Bowman, prevents stiffness by avoiding stagnant postures. Ergonomic adjustments, such as raising monitors to eye level and lowering keyboards, prevent neck and shoulder pain, according to ergonomist Meg Honan. These strategies aim to promote dynamic, adaptive postures rather than rigid 'correct' positions, as emphasized by physical therapists Leada Malek and Bowman. The tips are based on studies and practical tests involving over 20,000 participants.

item.title: California Preschool and TK Boost Reading, Math Skills by 11, 8 Months
item.description:
Source: LA Times Original headline: Preschool, transitional kindergarten deliver big: 11 months ahead in reading, 8 in math
California’s early education reforms, including preschool and transitional kindergarten (TK), boosted reading and math skills for children by third and fourth grades. A UC Berkeley study, commissioned by Stanford, found students who attended TK scored 11 months ahead in reading and 8 months ahead in math compared to peers without access. The 2010 law expanded TK to all 4-year-olds, with over half of eligible children enrolled in 2025. Researchers noted significant gains for low-income children, especially those from families with non-English-speaking parents, who saw math gains five times larger than average. Co-author Rucker Johnson emphasized the potential to identify and support children with untapped abilities. Teachers observed TK students were better prepared for classroom tasks, while others needed foundational skills taught in TK. The study, funded by multiple foundations, highlights the need for trained teachers as California scales TK. Researchers plan to track long-term outcomes, including college readiness, to assess lasting impacts of early education.

item.title: Japan's Aging Business Owners Sell to Young Entrepreneurs via Succession Platforms
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: Japan's aging business owners are selling their legacies for cheap to young entrepreneurs who are down to hustle
Japan's aging business owners are selling their enterprises to younger entrepreneurs through platforms like Relay and BATONZ, addressing succession challenges caused by low birth rates and an aging population. Kengo Ohama, 31, took over a café for free, retaining flexibility to redesign it. The Japan Finance Corporation reported 57.4% of small businesses expect closure without successors, up from 52.6% in 2019. Relay lists 900 businesses, with 350 active, while BATONZ has matched 3,421 pairs as of March 2026. Akitaka Mitsui, 67, sold his guesthouse to Kota Fujisawa, 29, after a stroke forced him to retire. Fujisawa, previously in consulting, now runs Local Knot Backpackers, paying less than 10 million yen. Takayuki Otawara, 29, bought a greenhouse for 3 million yen from a strawberry farmer to start a cacao farm. Succession platforms enable young entrepreneurs to access infrastructure, offering both challenges and rewards. Owners often prioritize transferring businesses to strangers over family heirs, creating opportunities for revitalization.

item.title: Edison's Creepy Talking Doll Once Celebrated on Edison Day
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: Culture Original headline: This was once Edison Day. We re-visit his creepy talking doll
Thomas Edison's 1890 talking dolls, featuring phonograph recordings, were marketed as novelties but quickly deemed failures. The dolls, 2 feet tall and weighing 4 pounds, had porcelain heads with large eyes and wooden limbs. Their voices were recorded by women in Edison's factory using wax cylinders, which warped after repeated use, rendering recordings unintelligible. Hal Wallace, a Smithsonian curator, noted the dolls' sensitivity to handling and their unsettling design, calling them 'little monsters.' Despite initial sales, the project ended within a month due to technical flaws and public reception. Edison's other innovations, like the electrical grid and research labs, overshadowed the dolls' legacy. Edison Day, once celebrated with parades, faded by the 1950s as technologies became commonplace. The dolls remain intriguing relics of early sound technology.

item.title: Most AI data centers may never be built due to 'bragawatts'
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: Most AI data centers may never be built. Blame the 'bragawatts.'
Most AI data centers announced may never be built, according to Bernstein Research. The firm analyzed over 7,000 US data center projects and found only 35% of the 500 gigawatts of planned capacity is likely to materialize. The rest, termed 'bragawatts,' are often from inexperienced newcomers with low credibility. Companies like O'Leary Digital, associated with investor Kevin O'Leary, scored 0.35 out of 5, with only 3% of its 15 gigawatts expected to be built. Joule Capital Partners and Vermaland also scored low, with Bernstein estimating 11% and 4% of their projects will proceed. Analysts note that many announcements lack construction progress or customer commitments. Established firms like Amazon, Google, and Microsoft score higher due to experience. The term 'bragawatts' originated in industry circles, though its origin is unclear. Speculative projects clog electricity grids, with Texas facing 450 gigawatts of demand, far exceeding its 85 gigawatt capacity. While some projects are genuine, many are placeholders or abandoned before construction. Bernstein and Aterio data suggest the AI infrastructure boom is real, but much of the announced capacity is not credible.

item.title: Germany's Government Sites Resume After PHP Security Patch
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Original headline: Germany news: Many sites back online after PHP security fix
German government and public service websites were taken offline overnight after a critical PHP security vulnerability was discovered. Over 20 MAN trucks were set on fire in Leipzig, prompting police to investigate possible arson linked to political motives. The Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) warned that AI-powered tools could enable widespread exploitation of the PHP flaw within hours of security patches being released, urging temporary internet disconnection for vulnerable sites. While some sites have resumed operations, officials cautioned that full security may take months, especially for outdated systems. Meanwhile, Germany's battery storage capacity rose by 8.2 gigawatt-hours in 2026, with a 91% increase in installations compared to 2025. The Interior Ministry reported a surge in far-right martial arts clubs, now numbering 20, up from 12 in 2024. BSW-Solar director Carsten Körnig highlighted battery storage as a key driver for Germany's energy transition, though faster expansion is needed to meet clean energy targets. The BSI also emphasized the risk of AI-driven attacks exploiting unpatched systems.

item.title: AI Safety Researchers Leave Tech Firms for Independent Work
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: The AI safety bottleneck: Save the world or get the bag
Rishub Jain left Google DeepMind to cofound Sampura Research, arguing that top AI companies are not investing enough in safety to justify his continued work at the lab. Jain claims companies like Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic prioritize safety but could do more, which inhibits his ability to focus on critical alignment research. Similar departures from OpenAI and Anthropic have raised alarms about the risks of unchecked AI development, with researchers warning of existential threats. AI safety roles have surged 91% on LinkedIn, driven by anticipated IPOs and philanthropy from groups like Coefficient Giving, which raised $50 million for AI safety startups. Despite growing funding, the field faces a talent shortage, with startups and nonprofits competing for experts in a narrow pool. Salaries for AI safety roles range from $273,000 to $395,000, far below offers from tech giants like Meta and Anthropic. Researchers debate whether working inside companies or independently is more effective, with some like David Robinson criticizing the lack of institutional checks in AI development. OpenAI recently fired three researchers for sharing data with safety experts, sparking concerns about internal safety practices. Philanthropists like Jaan Tallinn and Dustin Moskovitz are funneling billions into AI safety through grants and startups, aiming to prepare for a potential deluge of funding. The field now attracts more attention, with 80,000 Hours reporting over 8,000 career consultations since 2011, many focused on AI safety. Critics argue the focus on long-term risks may neglect immediate societal needs, but the urgency of AI development has accelerated investment and recruitment efforts.

item.title: Jane Doe writes to Cornell faculty as vote of no confidence looms
item.description:
Source: Washington Post Original headline: Jane Doe wrote to Cornell faculty as it considers vote of no confidence
Jane Doe, a woman suing Cornell University over alleged rape in 2024, wrote to faculty leaders expressing feeling unsupported by the administration. Her letter, obtained by The Washington Post, claims university president Michael Kotlikoff questioned why she delayed reporting the incident, which she interpreted as skepticism about her account. The faculty senate is set to debate a vote of no confidence in the administration amid international scrutiny of campus sexual assault cases. Cornell officials disputed Doe’s account, stating Kotlikoff’s question was directed at bystanders who didn’t use the anonymous tip line, not Doe. The university expelled or suspended some accused men and closed the fraternity chapter. Doe’s lawsuit alleges she was drugged and raped at a fraternity house, with no criminal charges filed. New York Governor Kathy Hochul appointed Letitia James as special prosecutor to investigate. Cornell’s dean shared Doe’s letter with an independent investigator hired to review sexual assault protocols.

item.title: Box Exec Prioritizes AI Skills and Side Projects in Hiring
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: This Box executive loves candidates with side projects. His own involves bringing back old-school TV.
Rand Wacker, Box's vice president of product strategy, said AI literacy is a baseline requirement for job candidates, but side projects demonstrate passion and innovation. He emphasized that prototyping ideas, rather than case studies, is now key in interviews. Candidates showcasing AI-built products, like mobile apps on the App Store, stand out. Wacker, who has spent 30 years in tech, shared his own side project: an Apple TV app using Cursor to revive old-school TV by randomly playing movies from his library. He criticized modern streaming decision fatigue, noting how AI tools now allow him to experiment with ideas he previously couldn't pursue. Wacker’s project highlights how executives are re-engaging with coding through AI to stay connected to product development. He argued that experimenting with AI enables deeper understanding of its applications in both personal and professional contexts.

item.title: Quilt Artist Wrongfully Sentenced to Death at 17 Receives Solo Exhibit
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: Culture Original headline: Sentenced to death at 17, at 68, quilt artist receives solo museum exhibition
Gary Tyler, a quilt artist, was wrongfully sentenced to death at 17 for a murder he did not commit. After spending 30 years in Louisiana's Angola prison, he was released in 2016 following a U.S. Supreme Court ruling that required states to resentence juvenile life inmates. Tyler's case involved a 1974 photo of him wearing a body shirt and bandana, which became a symbol of his innocence. Despite three pardon recommendations, Louisiana governors denied clemency. While incarcerated, Tyler created quilts for a hospice program, raising $30,000. His work, including 'The Tree of Life,' is now featured in a solo exhibit at the Grand Rapids Art Museum. Tyler criticizes the criminal justice system's bias against people of color and the poor, using his art to honor incarcerated individuals. The exhibit, 'Gary Tyler: Rebirth,' runs through January 3.

item.title: How long does it take to save up for a starter home? Twice as long as it did in 2019
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: News
A new analysis by the Center for Responsible Lending shows it now takes median-income renters 16 years to save for a starter home, double the 2019 timeframe. Rising home prices, inflation, and stagnant incomes have driven this increase. Black renters face even longer timelines, at 21 years. The report attributes this to higher home prices, inflation, and rising closing costs, including homeowners insurance. For middle-income households, savings periods have doubled to 12 years. Front-line workers now face 10-13 years to save. The analysis assumes a 3.5% down payment, lower than typical, and notes many families cannot save at all. Housing costs outpace incomes nationwide, with rural areas facing sharper affordability issues. The report calls for more down payment assistance, zoning reforms, and supply increases to address the gap. Despite challenges, homeownership remains a key wealth-building path for many families.

item.title: AI Generates Math Proofs, Challenges Mathematicians' Roles
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: Technology Original headline: AI is shaking up the field of mathematics. But what comes next?
OpenAI released over 370 mathematical results, including a solution to the Unique Games Conjecture, sparking challenges for mathematicians. Dana Moshkovitz of UT Austin called the AI-generated proof 'right' but noted the write-up was 'not made for human consumption.' Daniel Litt of the University of Toronto found a subtle error in an algebraic geometry paper, calling the AI output 'raw mathematical data' requiring human verification. Lean, a proof-checking program, identified discrepancies in OpenAI's proof of a Millennium Prize Problem, with Anders Hansen of Cambridge University highlighting a critical mismatch between natural language and Lean's formal logic. Anthropic and OpenAI pledged $5 million each to evaluate AI-assisted results, but mathematicians face a daunting task of reviewing thousands of poorly structured papers. Moshkovitz, who had dedicated years to solving the Unique Games Conjecture, now faces uncertainty about her career path as AI reshapes the field. The debate centers on whether AI's role in mathematics is a tool or a threat to traditional scholarly work.

item.title: Netflix Holds Earnings Call After Layoffs and Leadership Changes
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: Business Original headline: Netflix holds quarterly earnings call following leadership shakeup and layoffs
Netflix reported its third-quarter earnings, revealing the slowest revenue growth in three years. The company announced layoffs of over 1,000 employees and the departure of top executives, including content chief Bela Bajaria and chairman of Netflix Film. Co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters addressed investors, acknowledging the financial situation falls short of expectations. Peters stated, 'Our engagement is solid, but we know that we can do better.' Sarandos praised Bajaria's contributions before announcing Peter Rice, former 21st Century Fox president, as her replacement. Analyst Sean McNulty noted the broader Hollywood layoffs, citing Disney's recent cuts and upcoming Skydance layoffs. Netflix highlighted upcoming projects, including the limited series 'East Of Eden' and films like 'The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth,' alongside live sports events like the NFL and Women's World Cup.

item.title: Data Centers Spark Political and Environmental Debate
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic Original headline: The Data-Center Rebellion Is Just Beginning
Data centers have become a focal point of political and environmental debate as their scale and impact grow. These facilities, which power digital services, now demand hundreds of megawatts of electricity, comparable to a medium-sized city. Public opposition surged after the 2022 release of ChatGPT, with 75% of Americans opposing nearby projects. Senator Bernie Sanders called for a national moratorium, linking data centers to broader AI challenges, while Florida Governor Ron DeSantis pushed for state-level restrictions. Similar tensions emerged globally, with Singapore, Ireland, and the Netherlands imposing moratoriums in the late 2010s. Recent actions include Denmark downgrading data centers for grid priority and Thailand halting 49 projects. Political shifts in the U.S. and Europe reflect balancing AI adoption with public concerns over energy costs, environmental impact, and corporate influence. The November midterms could shape the future of the data-center boom, as communities and governments grapple with the infrastructure’s societal and environmental costs.

item.title: The Paradox at the Heart of China’s Export Boom
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy
China’s exports surged 36.3% year-over-year in September, the largest monthly jump since 2010, driven by AI demand, eased U.S. trade tensions, and domestic economic pressures. Despite a struggling domestic economy battered by the pandemic and real estate crisis, China’s manufacturing boom persists. Deflation at home boosted export competitiveness, while cheaper credit from the collapsing real estate sector funneled funds into manufacturing. High-end sectors like electric vehicles and smartphones dominate the growth. GDP growth this quarter exceeded expectations, likely reaching 4.6% annually, still below pre-pandemic levels. The government aims to rebalance supply and demand, but domestic weakness fuels the export surge. U.S. trade policies under Trump inadvertently supported China’s growth, while Europe may offer the strongest pushback. The paradox lies in China’s export success coexisting with weak GDP growth for its size.

item.title: AI Investments Fail to Deliver Measurable Productivity Gains
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Original headline: The Deployment Failure Holding Back Your AI Investments
Companies investing in AI are struggling to achieve measurable productivity gains. Research shows widespread AI adoption without significant impact. A 2026 survey of 6,000 executives found 69% use AI actively, yet 90% reported no effect on productivity or employment. McKinsey's 2025 analysis noted 88% of organizations use AI regularly, but only 39% saw enterprise-level EBIT impact. A separate 2025 study revealed just 5% of AI pilots delivered measurable bottom-line results. The issue stems from AI tools optimizing within individual functions rather than across organizational processes. This gap between investment and tangible outcomes persists despite growing AI adoption rates.

item.title: Xi’s Power Structure: Li and Cai as Key Lieutenants
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Original headline: Xi’s Gang of Three
Xi Jinping relies on Premier Li Qiang and Politburo Standing Committee member Cai Qi as his two most critical lieutenants to sustain his rule. Li oversees government affairs and ranks second in the party hierarchy, while Cai manages party operations, including the Secretariat and General Office of the CCP Central Committee, and holds key positions like the Central Party School. Together, they form what analysts describe as the 'central gang of three,' a framework to understand power dynamics rather than a faction akin to the historical Gang of Four. Unlike Lin Biao and Jiang Qing, who had independent political capital under Mao, Li and Cai derive authority solely from Xi’s trust. Cai’s proximity to Xi grants him influence, but party affairs remain under Xi’s direct control, with other loyalists handling specific domains like anti-corruption and personnel. Li, meanwhile, manages the State Council, handling economic and administrative tasks, though his authority is constrained by Xi’s oversight. Both men operate under Xi’s authority, with Cai’s role focused on implementing party directives and Li’s on governing the state. Recent appointments, such as Shi Taifeng’s transfer to the Organization Department, further limit Cai’s ability to consolidate power. The division of responsibilities ensures neither can challenge Xi’s dominance, balancing their roles to maintain stability within the CCP.

item.title: U.S. Military Overextended by Prolonged Deployments, Analysts Warn
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Original headline: A Less-Is-More Strategy for America
The USS Abraham Lincoln and its strike group returned to the U.S. after 320 days at sea, facing severe shortages, plumbing failures, and plummeting morale. Sailors reported water contamination and eight attempted suicides. Military analysts warn that prolonged deployments, combined with the Trump administration’s reallocation of Indo-Pacific forces to the Middle East, have strained the U.S. military’s capacity. The force was designed for short, decisive conflicts, not sustained global operations. Defense officials plan to expand the military and boost funding, but experts argue this is insufficient. Instead, they urge scaling back operations to focus on critical threats like China and Russia, reducing the burden on resources and personnel. The current strategy prioritizes high-end weapons for potential great-power wars, but overuse of forces has led to maintenance backlogs, declining readiness, and undercrewed ships. Congress may approve a $1.1 trillion base budget increase, but even this falls short of addressing systemic issues. Analysts suggest a more realistic approach would involve prioritizing key missions and reducing the scope of military involvement to avoid overextension.

item.title: West Coast Storm Signals Larger Weather Pattern Shift
item.description:
Source: Washington Post Original headline: Why a West Coast storm may be the start of something much bigger
A severe storm system approaching the West Coast on Wednesday is expected to bring heavy rain, thunderstorms, and rough seas to California and the Intermountain West. Flood watches are in effect for Southern California north of Los Angeles, Arizona, southern Utah, southwestern Colorado, and western New Mexico as the storm lingers through the weekend. NOAA’s Storm Prediction Center warned of a 'climatologically rare' severe storm risk, including tornadoes, large hail, and damaging winds, with a Level 3 (out of 5) risk in Arizona’s Phoenix to Flagstaff corridor. Coastal Southern and Central California, including Los Angeles, face tornado threats. The National Weather Service noted potential beach erosion and tidal overflows in Malibu and Long Beach, areas recently hit by Tropical Storm Rachel. Record warm seas near the coast are expected to increase storm moisture through winter. A strong El Niño in the Pacific is driving upper-atmosphere winds near Hawaii, fueling a subtropical jet stream pattern that may lead to more stormy weather in the U.S. during November. The storm is seen as a precursor to broader weather changes.

item.title: Trial closing arguments begin for man accused in 2012 UNC student death
item.description:
Source: ABC News: Top Stories Original headline: Closing arguments set in trial of man accused of killing UNC student in 2012
Closing arguments are set for Thursday in the trial of Miguel Salguero Olivares, accused of killing UNC student Faith Hedgepeth in 2012. Hedgepeth, 19, was beaten to death in her off-campus apartment in September 2012. Olivares, 33, was arrested in 2021 after providing a DNA sample matching evidence from the crime scene. He faces first-degree murder, rape, and burglary charges. Prosecutors allege he killed Hedgepeth in a fit of rage, citing DNA found on a bloodied rum bottle, in her body, and on a fast-food bag. Forensic scientist Erin Ermish testified DNA evidence showed a 170 septillion likelihood of Hedgepeth and Olivares being the source, compared to an unknown individual. Defense attorneys challenged the DNA evidence, questioning witness accounts and crime scene procedures. Jurors wept after viewing autopsy photos, and Olivares cried during a jailhouse call playback. The trial, which began in October, saw over two dozen prosecution witnesses, including friends, law enforcement, and a DNA expert. Olivares did not testify, and his defense rested without calling witnesses.

item.title: Karl Bushby completes 28-year foot journey from Chile to England
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: Culture Original headline: He left Chile on foot to England 28 years ago. He's almost finally home
Karl Bushby, a British adventurer, has completed a 28-year journey from Chile to England on foot, nearly finishing his quest. He began the trek in 1996, walking without transportation or returning home until reaching England. Inspired by a father's birthday card recounting a Special Forces debate on walking from London to New York via the Bering Strait, Bushby extended the challenge. His 'Goliath Expedition' included crossing the Darién Gap jungle, the Bering Strait, and overcoming financial setbacks, visa denials, and logistical hurdles. Bushby recently swam the English Channel after being barred from the Channel Tunnel, reuniting with his mother in Hull. He acknowledged the personal cost, including strained family relationships and a granddaughter he's never met. 'Keep it within a reasonable time frame,' he advised, warning of the toll on relationships. Now, he reflects on reestablishing himself in his home country after years of travel.

item.title: Russia to Resume U.S.-Mediated Ukraine Peace Talks Amid Strategic Hurdles
item.description:
Source: BBC News, FP Foreign Policy Original headline: Russia Agrees to Resume Ukraine Peace Talks Amid Diplomatic Efforts and Strategic Considerations
Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to resume U.S.-mediated peace talks with Ukraine as soon as next month, though negotiations will remain technical, according to U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff. Russian officials, including foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov, criticized Western and Ukrainian proposals as lacking 'useful' solutions, while emphasizing progress is 'moving in that direction.' The talks in St. Petersburg and Oslo, led by Witkoff and European representatives, were described as 'good and constructive' by Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre. However, a trilateral meeting between Putin, Zelensky, and Trump has not occurred. Witkoff acknowledged 'important work remains' but claimed Trump remains committed to ending the war. Ukraine’s Zelensky agreed to freeze its front line but continued striking Russian energy infrastructure. Trump, who paused sanctions on Russian diesel, doubted Zelensky’s willingness to end the conflict. Analysts suggest Putin may leverage growing ties with China, with a potential meeting between Putin, Trump, and Chinese President Xi Jinping at the Apec summit in November. Russia insists on maintaining territorial gains, while Ukraine demands security guarantees, leaving the stalemate unresolved. The Trump administration called the efforts 'constructive,' despite no concrete progress.

item.title: Couple opens raccoon rehab center, saves 800 so far
item.description:
Source: Washington Post Original headline: This couple opened a rehab for raccoons. They’ve saved 800 so far.
Paul and Sarah Bookbinder opened a raccoon rehabilitation center in 2018 after taking in two injured kits nine years earlier. They sold their home to fund the 53-acre facility in Earlville, New York, and have since saved over 800 raccoons. The couple, who named their first two kits Stanley and Laurel, faced heartbreak when the animals died, prompting them to dedicate their lives to wildlife care. They bottle-feed newborn kits up to eight times daily, transition them to natural foods at three months, and release them in late summer or fall when they show independence. The Bookbinders, who describe raccoons as intelligent and resilient, have also cared for injured raccoons unable to survive in the wild, including those with physical disabilities. They engrave each raccoon’s name—alive or deceased—on rocks in a garden, now expanded due to the number of animals saved. The couple’s commitment includes sacrificing vacations and sleep, with Sarah noting, 'We’re not the ones that matter. The raccoons are the ones that matter.' They plan to release their final group of the year, adding six new names to the garden.

item.title: The Atlantic Releases List of 50 Unforgettable Love Stories
item.description: Source: The Atlantic Original headline: The Atlantic Publishes List of “50 Unforgettable Love Stories” The Atlantic launched '50 Unforgettable Love Stories,' a curated list of romantic narratives spanning over four centuries. The selection includes works from 1591 to 2024, featuring novels, poetry, plays, and short stories. The list was compiled by The Atlantic’s Books team, who gathered input from scholars, librarians, critics, and authors to identify standout titles written in English. The editors emphasized that love stories, while often associated with romance genres, also appear in works by authors like Arundhati Roy, Anne Carson, and Beverly Jenkins. The project is part of The Atlantic’s Books section, which includes other initiatives like '65 Essential Children’s Books' and 'The Great American Novels.' The list aims to highlight love stories as enduring literary themes that reflect both personal and universal experiences.

item.title: AI agents tested on email, lunch orders, and website building
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: I put Muse, Dot, and Instinct to the test. There was a clear winner, but not because it worked best.
Muse, Dot, and Instinct were tested on email triage, lunch orders, and website building. Muse, the only free agent, excelled at email triage by filtering important messages. Dot identified a critical tax-related email exchange, saving the user from potential issues. Instinct found a missed event invitation but faced usability challenges with text-based interactions. Ordering lunch proved problematic for all: Muse accidentally used an HSA-linked card, Instinct required multiple text messages, and Dot struggled with login steps. Website design tasks produced generic, unappealing mockups, with Dot's design being the most polished but featuring awkward copy. The author concluded that none of the agents reliably simplified tasks, and managing multiple agents caused confusion. The user recommends against using multiple AI agents simultaneously, citing the hassle of coordination and lack of clear benefits beyond basic automation.

item.title: 42-Year-Old Travel Journalist Moves to Montreal After Lease Ends
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: Newly single and 42, I left Connecticut for Montreal on a whim. People told me I was brave.
A 42-year-old travel journalist left her Connecticut home for Montreal after her lease ended and rent rose to $3,250 monthly. A friend's offer of a cheaper Canadian apartment prompted the move. She now lives in a 900-square-foot unit for $775 monthly, including utilities. The decision followed a lease ending, relationship ending, and financial pressures. She learned to row and explores Montreal's culture, including its markets and restaurants. While facing loneliness, she finds comfort in new friendships and proximity to family. She reflects on being called 'brave' despite feeling it was a practical choice.

item.title: NATO 3.0 Is a Dangerous Gamble
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy
The Trump administration’s NATO 3.0 plan risks undermining both conventional and nuclear deterrence. Launched by Elbridge Colby, the policy aims to reduce U.S. conventional forces in Europe while maintaining nuclear guarantees. Troop withdrawals include 5,000 from Germany, potential 25,000-40,000 departures, and cuts to the NATO Force Model by one-third to one-half. U.S. plans to reduce aircraft, warships, and drones in Europe, shifting focus to nuclear deterrence. Colby argues this rebalancing would let Europe handle conventional defense while Washington manages nuclear threats. However, analysts warn this creates vulnerabilities: Europe’s inability to defend itself conventionally, erosion of U.S. nuclear credibility, and proliferation risks. The Financial Times reports U.S. plans to expand nuclear basing beyond six host nations. Critics argue splitting conventional and nuclear responsibilities complicates escalation management, as Russia’s doctrine anticipates counterforce strikes. Europe’s lack of long-range strike capabilities, like Tomahawk or Dark Eagle missiles, further weakens its position. Meanwhile, European nations like France and the UK are advancing nuclear cooperation, potentially undermining U.S. influence. NATO 3.0’s goal to encourage burden-sharing without proliferation faces risks of backfiring, as European states may seek independent nuclear options. The plan’s abrupt cuts and lack of phased reductions could destabilize alliance cohesion and deterrence.

item.title: Climate Change Drives Migration to Cooler Northern Regions
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: World Original headline: Meet the people moving north to escape increasingly hot summers
Mike Coe and his partner moved to Scotland's Isle of Skye after realizing the UK's Midlands would become too hot. Coe, 69, noted southern regions faced record heat this summer, with five consecutive heatwaves and drought, while Skye remained temperate. Susan Chinnery and Steve Lewis relocated to the Orkney Islands after enduring unbearable summers in Milton Keynes, recalling 2022's heat akin to 1976. Melissa Terras moved to Edinburgh in 2017, citing climate change, and now sees more people considering similar moves. Real estate agents in Scotland report increased demand for cooler climates. Scientists note Europe is the fastest-warming continent, with 35,000 excess deaths linked to heat. Gaia Vince predicts climate change will drive mass migration to temperate regions like northern Scotland, Alaska, and parts of New Zealand. Jason Sorensen, a California native, moved to Scotland after wildfires and extreme heat in the U.S. The trend reflects growing adaptation to climate impacts, with Scotland's housing prices rising while southern England's fall. U.N. officials warn of escalating climate crises, urging preparedness.
